title: Nelson Rosario on Decentralized AI: An Alternative to Big Tech or a Complimentary Approach?
author: Nelson Rosario

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Rosario does not engage the cluster’s proposition about jagged legal-task capability, verification, human expertise or workflow redesign. He instead shifts the priority to AI infrastructure concentration, continuity of access and decentralizing compute, models or data to reduce control points.
qs: Again, it comes back to kind of like the choke points of any application that leverages the Internet and is not run locally, right?

So that's why I think you can't really, it's really hard to give a tight definition of what decentralized AI is, because it very much depends upon the perspective of the company or the individual that's looking at it, right?

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The excerpt contains only closing announcements, possible rebranding and contact guidance. It offers no substantive claims or evidence about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation, implementation practices or autonomous workflows, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports technology-enabled legal delivery through Percipient’s claim that legal professionals, technology, project management and human oversight can increase efficiency and capacity. However, this is promotional and provides no measured evidence that freed capacity is redirected to strategic work; the decentralized-AI discussion is largely unrelated to the cluster proposition.
qs: By combining legal expertise and technology, Percipient enables legal teams to get more work done for less.
Our team of legal professionals leverage tech and project management principles with the right amount of human oversight to deliver precise, efficient, and cost-effective legal solutions.

kp.k: Decentralized AI prioritizes access rather than a settled architecture
kp.d: Rosario argues that decentralized AI lacks a settled definition: decentralization could concern individual layers of an application rather than its entire stack. He interprets its central objective as censorship-resistant access to models, compute and data, protecting users and applications against a single provider cutting them off. This is a proposed design objective, not evidence of an achieved system.
qs: Does every single layer have to be decentralized, running by itself, not owned by the same company? Is that what we mean by decentralization?
So I think what people are actually aiming for with the AI is censorship resistance, whether they realize it or not

the big fears are somebody locking up the models, so nobody knows how they work, somebody locking down all the compute, so you can't actually run any queries or interact with these AI apps, and somebody locking up all the data.

kp.k: Decentralized systems may complement rather than displace major providers
kp.d: Asked by host Chad Main how decentralization can compete with well-funded technology companies, Rosario does not claim it can overcome them. He instead envisages parallel, complementary systems assembled from separate infrastructure components. He identifies robust decentralized physical infrastructure as a condition for realizing this vision and centralized hosting as a continuing point of vulnerability.
qs: Well, I don't know that it can overcome it, right? I think it can be a complimentary set of systems that exist in parallel, and the only way that they can do that is by chopping it up, right?
So D-PIN is something that needs to become really robust for decentralized AI applications to really exist the way that they're meant to exist, right?
Is if AWS shuts down your account, that's it.

kp.k: Existing protocols supply pieces, not a demonstrated complete solution
kp.d: Rosario names Filecoin and Arweave as decentralized storage offerings that supply part of the infrastructure. He describes Bitensor, as transcribed, as the largest decentralized-AI player and also mentions HyperCycle and smaller token-funded startups, without supplying market-share figures. His suggestion that model components could run across different services is explicitly tentative rather than a reported implementation.
qs: Filecoin is an application that offers decentralized storage, Arweave.
So some of the applications that already exist, and companies that are protocols that already exist, offer some part of the solution to all of this.
I mean, Bitensor is really the biggest one, because they have been thinking about this the longest.
But you could break it up into component parts that then have to reach out to the other part of the model, which is stored elsewhere, right?

kp.k: Industry coordination targets standards, policy, community and capital
kp.d: Rosario describes the society's four priorities as engineering best practices, policy advocacy, community building and capital formation. He compares its proposed standards function to the Internet Engineering Task Force and argues that scarce conferences constrain knowledge exchange. Main's introduction identifies the organization as the newly renamed Advanced AI Society; Rosario uses its earlier Decentralized AI Society name during the interview.
qs: Engineering, trying to develop best practices with respect to all of this.
You could think of that part as akin to the Internet Engineering Task Force that puts out standards for operating on the web.
Policy, which is really making sure that the society is helping members to advocate for policy that doesn't strangle the industry before it's even got off the ground.
It's hard for people to come together and trade war stories or best practices or get an understanding of the trends in the industry.

kp.k: Public-goods characteristics complicate decentralized AI financing
kp.d: Rosario argues that startups supplying parts of a decentralized stack often resemble public-goods builders, making funding and value propositions difficult, although he acknowledges possible subscription models. An accelerator and a member-participating venture fund are ideas under discussion, not established initiatives or demonstrated financing solutions.
qs: they're sort of building public goods more than they're building like, I mean, I suppose you can do it as a subscription model or something else, right?
The point is the worry is that they'll be difficult to fund, right?
there's been conversations around trying to do some sort of accelerator, put together some sort of actual venture fund that members could participate in and help identify kind of opportunities.

kp.d: Rosario considers permissionless technology beneficial over the long term but argues that powerful states increasingly perceive unrestricted access as risky. He invokes US policymakers' reaction to the release called DeepSeq in the transcript as an illustration, rather than presenting systematic policy evidence. The feasibility of permissionless, open-source AI remains an open question in his account.
qs: permissionless tech is becoming, I would argue, a much riskier proposition for the most powerful countries in the world to tolerate, right?
if you can't prevent people from using the technology you're building, is, I think, a great thing because I think long term, it's very positive
But it's more so how exactly, or is it possible or feasible to build out these permissionless open-source AI solutions that people are just calling DAI for now?

kp.k: Independent agents could require permissionless data and model access
kp.d: Rosario offers a hypothetical agent that receives cryptocurrency and then obtains necessary data independently, contrasting this with subscribing to a provider's predefined bots. He argues that conventional account-signup requirements obstruct that scenario, making permissionless data and potentially models important. He does not report a deployed agent or a legal-services application.
qs: Instead, you can just, for example, send crypto to an address that an AI agent controls.
Well, that AI agent then needs to get some data or something, right?
So it needs access to data that exists, in a permissionless fashion, perhaps same thing with models, you know, just really depends.

kp.k: Nonprofit associations can facilitate regulatory and industry engagement
kp.d: Drawing on his experience establishing the Illinois Blockchain Association, Rosario reports that conversations became easier once officials recognized an industry-wide nonprofit interlocutor. He hopes the AI society can similarly facilitate discussions with regulators, elected officials and large technology companies. His report of interest from unnamed major technology companies is anecdotal and does not establish commitments.
qs: Well, this year, those conversations became a lot easier because there was an industry association.
they're advocating for the industry, but they're not advocating for one individual company
some of those big tech players have already reached out and are interested

kp.k: Growing AI dependence raises the stakes of provider exclusion
kp.d: Rosario attributes AI's acceleration to available cloud compute, large datasets and transformer architecture, and identifies the November 2022 public beta of ChatGPT as a consumer-facing turning point. He argues that AI now operates as consumer and industrial technology simultaneously, and predicts that increasing everyday dependence will make continued access more important. This is a broad technological framing rather than measured evidence of legal-market change.
qs: once CHAT GPT went public 2022 in November, the public beta, now it became consumer facing, right?
It's now become consumer tech and industrial tech at the same time.
as people become more and more dependent on using AI tools in their everyday life, we more and more don't want them to be cut off from those tools, right?

kp.k: Lawyers' fabricated citations illustrate dangers of uncritical AI reliance
kp.d: Rosario cites reports of lawyers filing briefs containing nonexistent cases as examples of blindly trusting AI output; he supplies no named cases, counts or measured error rates. Using Dune as an analogy, he distinguishes creating intelligent machines from surrendering human thinking to them. Main separately emphasizes teaching lawyers that AI can invent material.
qs: I don't think that AI is necessarily has to be antagonistic to human beings. But I think it would be really problematic for people to just blindly trust AI, which we're already seeing happen.
in the legal space, there's been multiple stories of lawyers filing briefs with cases that don't exist because it was an AI output, right?
The Cardinal sin that led to the Butlarian Jihad and why there's no AI in Dune Universe was man turning over thinking to machines.

kp.k: Foundational AI literacy should precede specialized lawyer education
kp.d: Rosario reports that the Illinois State Bar Association Standing Committee on AI initially focuses on CLE and other educational content. He advocates beginning with the basics lawyers need to formulate their own questions, including questions addressed to AI tools. His mechanism is that missing foundational knowledge prevents lawyers from recognizing what to ask and contributes to avoidable mistakes; no educational outcomes are reported.
qs: The main focus of that Standing Committee, at least initially, is creating CLE content, articles, blog posts, and everything else.
I was advocating that we should really start with like, what are the basics that a lawyer needs to know, so that they can figure out how to ask their own questions.
But if you don't know a topic exists, because you don't have the base layer knowledge to ask the right questions, then of course, it's easy to make mistakes that look really dumb in hindsight.

kp.k: AI productivity gains may coexist with diminished independent thinking
kp.d: Rosario speculates that extensive delegation to AI could reduce creativity while increasing productivity, depending on its measurement. He also raises concerns about relationships with AI bots and hopes for more intentional technology use, acknowledging the educational burden. These are predictions about human behavior, not empirical findings or quantified forecasts for lawyers.
qs: if they're thinking less for themselves because they're using AI to do everything, creativity is going to go down.
Productivity, depending on how you measure it, may go up.
There's big fear of relationships with AI bots.
My hope is that people can become more intentional about their use of technology, but that's a heavy educational lift too.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rosario identifies blind reliance on AI as an existing source of errors in legal filings and advocates foundational AI education for lawyers.
pts.d: Nelson Rosario says lawyers have filed briefs containing nonexistent cases because they trusted AI output. Drawing on his participation in the Illinois State Bar Association Standing Committee on AI, he argues that lawyers need basic knowledge to formulate their own questions and avoid mistakes. This is a claim about reliance and professional learning, not a prediction of lawyer replacement or a quantified productivity gain. He also predicts that wider delegation of thinking to AI could reduce creativity while potentially increasing productivity, depending on its measurement.

pts.k: Rosario presents decentralized AI as a possible complement to centralized providers, aimed at preserving access to compute, data and models rather than necessarily defeating Big Tech.
pts.d: The interview's main domain is AI infrastructure. Rosario interprets decentralization's practical objective as censorship resistance: preventing a single provider from cutting off an application or controlling access to essential resources. He says parallel, complementary systems may be possible by dividing the technology stack, but robust decentralized physical infrastructure is a prerequisite. He does not claim that decentralized AI already has a settled architecture or can overcome large providers' financial advantages. He further proposes that independently operating AI agents could need permissionless data and potentially model access because they cannot use conventional account-registration arrangements.

pts.k: Rosario anticipates financing and policy obstacles for permissionless AI infrastructure and sees industry associations as a way to improve coordination and credibility.
pts.d: Rosario says decentralized AI infrastructure startups may be difficult to fund because they resemble public goods and their value propositions are hard for conventional investors to understand. He argues that geopolitical competition makes permissionless technology more politically sensitive, although he views it positively over the long term. He describes the society's engineering, policy, community-building and capital-formation work as intended to address these problems. An accelerator and venture fund are possibilities under discussion, not established funding outcomes. His expectation that an association can facilitate engagement with policymakers and large technology companies draws partly on his blockchain advocacy experience.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers anecdotal examples, Rosario's professional experience and infrastructure analogies, rather than quantitative evidence.
pts.d: For legal risks, Rosario refers to multiple stories of nonexistent cases in briefs without identifying cases, sanctions decisions or measured error rates. His educational recommendation draws on a recent bar committee meeting. For decentralization, he cites Filecoin and Arweave as existing storage components and identifies Bitensor and HyperCycle as participants; these examples are not demonstrations of a fully decentralized AI system. His association argument draws on his reported experience with the Illinois Blockchain Association and unnamed Big Tech expressions of interest. His predictions about cognition and society are reasoned concerns, illustrated through Dune, not empirical findings. No benchmarks, market-share figures, funding statistics or legal productivity studies are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Legal reliance errors are described as current; decentralized infrastructure and broader social changes are prospective and conditional, with no firm implementation timetable.
pts.d: In this 2025 source, Rosario describes AI-related filing errors as already occurring and foundational lawyer education as an initial committee priority. Decentralized AI is nascent, its definition unsettled and its feasibility dependent on infrastructure, finance and policy. The agent example is hypothetical. The creativity prediction is conditional on people surrendering thinking to AI, and the productivity prediction explicitly depends on measurement. Rosario expects long-run transformation but acknowledges uncertainty about its form. In a separate response about brain-chip integration, he gives a five-to-fifty-year range; that range should not be treated as a forecast for legal-services transformation or decentralized AI deployment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include practicing lawyers, AI application developers, infrastructure startups, investors, policymakers and people increasingly dependent on AI.
pts.d: Lawyers face mistakes from uncritical reliance and a need for foundational learning; Rosario does not distinguish law-firm sizes, seniority levels or legal practice markets. Developers could gain alternatives to restrictive centralized contracts and service cutoffs. Decentralized infrastructure startups face uncertain financing, while investors must understand unfamiliar public-good-like propositions. Regulators and elected officials are prospective interlocutors for industry associations. The public, including students, may face consequences from reduced independent thinking and dependence on AI tools. The transcript's Percipient advertisement is a host's promotional claim and is not attributed to Rosario or treated as evidence of AI-driven legal cost savings.
